verses.zh: 国民立约西亚的儿子约哈斯在耶路撒冷接续他父作王。
verses.en: The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in his father’s place in Jerusalem.[NOTE:1]
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
36:1 "the people of the land" See note at 2 Chr. 33:25.

"Joahaz" In 2 Kgs. 23:31, he is called by his full name, "Jehoahaz."

verses.zh: 约哈斯登基的时候年二十三岁，在耶路撒冷作王三个月。
verses.en: Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 埃及王在耶路撒冷废了他，又罚犹大国银子一百他连得，金子一他连得。
verses.en: The king of Egypt prevented him from ruling in Jerusalem and imposed on the land a special tax[NOTE:1] of 100 talents[NOTE:2] of silver and a talent of gold.
notes: Or “a fine.”

The Hebrew word כִּכַּר (kikkar, “circle”) refers generally to something that is round. When used of metals it can refer to a disk-shaped weight made of the metal or, by extension, to a standard unit of weight. According to the older (Babylonian) standard the “talent” weighed 130 lbs. (58.9 kg), but later this was lowered to 108.3 lbs. (49.1 kg). More recent research suggests the “light” standard talent was 67.3 lbs. (30.6 kg). Using this as the standard for calculation, the weight of the silver was 6,730 lbs. (3,060 kg).

36:3 "talents" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES.

verses.zh: 埃及王尼哥立约哈斯的哥哥以利雅敬作犹大和耶路撒冷的王，改名叫约雅敬，又将约哈斯带到埃及去了。
verses.en: The king of Egypt made Jehoahaz’s[NOTE:1] brother Eliakim king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Necho seized his brother Jehoahaz and took him to Egypt.
notes: Heb “his”; the referent (Jehoahaz) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary: 36:4 "Eliakim. . .Jehoiakim" Judean kings often took a throne name.

verses.zh: 约雅敬登基的时候年二十五岁，在耶路撒冷作王十一年，行耶和华―他　神眼中看为恶的事。
verses.en: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned for eleven years in Jerusalem.[NOTE:1] He did evil in the sight of[NOTE:2] the Lord his God.
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “in the eyes of.”
verses.commentary:
36:5 "and he did evil in the sight of the Lord his God" This is a recurrent phrase
which implies disobedience to the Mosaic covenant (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:32). In Jer. 26:20-24 we see his treatment of YHWH's
prophets. He imprisoned Jeremiah and Baruch (Jer. 36:26). Also notice how his actions affected the people in 2 Chr. 36:16.

verses.zh: 巴比伦王尼布甲尼撒上来攻击他，用铜链锁着他，要将他带到巴比伦去。
verses.en: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacked him,[NOTE:1] bound him with bronze chains, and carried him away[NOTE:2] to Babylon.
notes: Heb “came up against him.”
Heb “to carry him away.”
verses.commentary:
36:6 In 2 Kgs. 24:2 YHWH sends several invaders into Judah because of Jehoiakim's faithlessness
(and Manasseh's, 2 Chr. 36:3).

- bands of Chaldeans

- bands of Syrians

- bands of Moabites

- bands of Ammonites

"Nebuchadnezzar" The name (BDB 613) in Babylonian has several possible meanings.

- "Nebo, protect (the) boundary (or frontier)"

- "Nebo, protect (my) progeny"

- "Nebo, protect (my) inheritance"

- "Nebo, protect (the) crown"

- "Nebo, protect (thy) servant"

In Daniel, like Jeremiah, it is spelled two ways, Nebuchadrezzar (most accurate spelling) and Nebuchadnezzar
(found in OT 27 times). The difference is due to the transliteration from Babylonian to Aramaic/Hebrew. But why both spellings
are in one book is uncertain, possibly different scribes were used. The original name in Akkadian would have been Nabu-kudurri-usur.

He was not really king yet because his father Nabopolassar (626-605 b.c.) did not die until the summer of
605 b.c. He was the crown prince in charge of the military campaign. We have no other historical record of this raid. However,
2 Kgs. 24:1-7 and 2 Chr. 36:1-7 surely imply a confrontation between Nebuchadnezzar and Jehoiakim before 597 b.c.
Jerusalem seems to have fallen into Babylonian hands in 605 b.c. (Daniel and his friends taken), 597 b.c. (Jehoiachim and
nobles and artisans taken), 586 b.c. (general deportation) and 582 b.c. (all who could be found taken).

verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒又将耶和华殿里的器皿带到巴比伦，放在他神的庙里（或译：自己的宫里）。
verses.en: Nebuchadnezzar took some of the items in the Lord’s temple to Babylon and put them in his palace[NOTE:1] there.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “temple.”
Heb “in Babylon.” Repeating the proper name “Babylon” here would be redundant in contemporary English, so “there” has been used in the translation.
verses.commentary:
36:7 Nebuchadnezzar displayed his military victories by putting the idols and implements of the different gods of the
conquered nations in alcoves of the temple of Marduk (cf. Ezra 1:7).

He also took young men from each nation and turned them into servants in his great hall. They were trophies
(i.e., Daniel 9:1-4)!

verses.zh: 约雅敬其余的事和他所行可憎的事，并他一切的行为，都写在以色列和犹大列王记上。他儿子约雅斤接续他作王。
verses.en: The rest of the events of Jehoiakim’s reign, including the horrible sins he committed and his shortcomings, are recorded in the Scroll of the Kings of Israel and Judah.[NOTE:1] His son Jehoiachin replaced him as king.
notes: Heb “As for the rest of the events of Jehoiakim, and his horrible deeds which he did and that which was found against him, look, they are written on the scroll of the kings of Israel and Judah.”

verses.zh: 约雅斤登基的时候年八岁（在列王下二十四章八节是十八岁），在耶路撒冷作王三个月零十天，行耶和华眼中看为恶的事。
verses.en: Jehoiachin was eighteen[NOTE:1] years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem.[NOTE:2] He did evil in the sight of[NOTE:3] the Lord.
notes: The Hebrew text reads “eight,” but some ancient textual witnesses, as well as the parallel text in 2 Kgs 24:8, have “eighteen.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “in the eyes of.”
verses.commentary:
36:9

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, REB
"eight"

TEV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta
"eighteen"

The MT has "eight" which the UBS Text Project, p. 490, gives a "B" rating (some doubt). The older age
comes from 2 Kgs. 24:8 and the ancient versions and some Hebrew MSS.

The MT has "eight," which is apparently an ancient scribal error (i.e., "ten," BDB 797 dropped out of the text).

- eight (BDB 1032) ‒ שׁמנה

- eighteen (i.e., "eight" and "ten") ‒
שׁמנה

עשׂרה

See Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 214-215.

verses.zh: 过了一年，尼布甲尼撒差遣人将约雅斤和耶和华殿里各样宝贵的器皿带到巴比伦，就立约雅斤的叔叔（原文是兄）西底家作犹大和耶路撒冷的王。
verses.en: At the beginning of the year King Nebuchadnezzar ordered him to be brought[NOTE:1] to Babylon, along with the valuable items in the Lord’s temple. In his place Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiachin’s relative[NOTE:2] Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.
notes: Heb “sent and brought him.”

Heb “and he made Zedekiah his brother king.” According to the parallel text in 2 Kgs 24:17, Zedekiah was Jehoiachin’s uncle, not his brother. Therefore many interpreters understand אח (ʾakh) here in its less specific sense of “relative” (NEB “made his father’s brother Zedekiah king”; NASB “made his kinsman Zedekiah king”; NIV “made Jehoiachin’s uncle, Zedekiah, king”; NRSV “made his brother Zedekiah king”).
verses.commentary:
36:10 There were several deportations from Judah to Babylon (see Contextual Insights, C).

- 605 b.c.

- 597 b.c.

- 586 b.c.

- 582 b.c.

NASB, JPSOA
"his kinsman"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta
"brother"

TEV
"his uncle"

REB, LXX
"his father's brother"

The MT has "brother" (BDB 26) but 2 Kgs. 24:17 calls him "uncle." The Hebrew term "brother" can
mean "relative" (cf. Gen. 13:8; 14:14,16; 29:12,15; Num. 16:10; 18:2,6; 2 Sam. 19:12-13; 2 Chr. 22:8).

verses.zh: 西底家登基的时候年二十一岁，在耶路撒冷作王十一年，
verses.en: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem.[NOTE:1]
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 行耶和华―他　神眼中看为恶的事。先知耶利米以耶和华的话劝他，他仍不在耶利米面前自卑。
verses.en: He did evil in the sight of[NOTE:1] the Lord his God. He did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, the Lord’s spokesman.
notes: Heb “in the eyes of.”
verses.commentary:
36:12 Babylon left some of the very poor farmers and herdsmen to tend the fields and herds for taxation purposes
(cf. 2 Kgs. 24:14; 25:12).

"he did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet" In 2 Chronicles there are two VERBS
that reveal the hearts of the kings.

- humble (see notes at 2 Chr. 7:14; 12:6,7)

- seek (see notes at 2 Chr. 7:14; 15:4,15)

This last series of kings did neither, even though YHWH addressed them through his prophet Jeremiah. They
were exactly opposite to Hezekiah (cf. 2 Chr. 32:26; 33:12,23) and Josiah (cf. 2 Chr. 34:27).

verses.zh: 尼布甲尼撒曾使他指着　神起誓，他却背叛，强项硬心，不归服耶和华―以色列的　神。
verses.en: He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him vow allegiance[NOTE:1] in the name of God. He was stubborn and obstinate and refused to return[NOTE:2] to the Lord God of Israel.
notes: Or “made him swear an oath.”
Heb “and he stiffened his neck and strengthened his heart from returning.”
verses.commentary:
36:13 Notice the evil of Zedekiah and Judah.

- He broke his oath in YHWH's name (i.e., vassal oath probably on the names of several gods; breaking an oath to God
was a serious sin, cf. Ezek. 17:11-21).

- He stiffened his neck ‒ cf. Deut. 9:6,13; 10:16; 31:27; 2 Chr. 30:8; Neh. 9:16,17,29; Jer. 7:26; 17:23; 19:15.

- He hardened his heart (i.e., he trusted Egypt, not YHWH).

- All his officials of the priests were very unfaithful.

- All the people were very unfaithful (v. 16).

The "unfaithfulness" of the priests and people is highlighted by the PARTICIPLE and
NOUN of the same root (BDB 591, KB 612).

Notice how the Chronicler does not mention the unfaithfulness of the Levites. He is supportive of them
throughout the book.

verses.zh: 众祭司长和百姓也大大犯罪，效法外邦人一切可憎的事，污秽耶和华在耶路撒冷分别为圣的殿。
verses.en: All the leaders of the priests and people became more unfaithful and committed the same horrible sins practiced by the nations.[NOTE:1] They defiled the Lord’s temple which he had consecrated in Jerusalem.
notes: Heb “like all the abominable practices of the nations.”
verses.commentary:
36:14 "the people were very unfaithful" This is am emphatic phrase.

- BDB 915, KB 1176, Hiphil PERFECT ‒ "very" or "exceedingly"

- BDB 591, KB 612, both Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT and NOUN ‒ "unfaithful"

The VERB (BDB 915, KB 1176) is used three times in 2 Chronicles to show the Judean
kings' evil (which influenced the whole nation) and caused YHWH to unleash the "curses" of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.

- Manasseh ‒ 2 Chr. 33:6

- Amon ‒ 2 Chr. 33:23

- Zedekiah led the priests and people to continue their idolatry ‒ 2 Chr. 36:14

Judgment was the only option of God's word and God's character is true! The powerful statement in Galatians 6:7,
people and nations reap what they sow!

"all the abominations of the nations" This phrase repeatedly refers to idolatry (cf. Deut. 18:9; 1 Kgs. 1424;
2 Kgs. 16:3; 21:2; 2 Chr. 33:2; 36:14; Ezek. 8:10-16 lists the kinds of idolatry; see exegetical notes online). See the
terrible list in Deut. 18:9-13,14; also Leviticus 20; see exegetical notes online.

verses.zh: 耶和华―他们列祖的　神因为爱惜自己的民和他的居所，从早起来差遣使者去警戒他们。
verses.en: The Lord God of their ancestors[NOTE:1] continually warned them through his messengers,[NOTE:2] for he felt compassion for his people and his dwelling place.
notes: Heb “fathers.”
Heb “and the Lord God of their fathers sent against them by the hand of his messengers, getting up early and sending.”
verses.commentary:
36:15 The prophets (i.e., "again and again," highlighted by the IMPERFECT VERB and
INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root, BDB 1018, KB 1511) were sent in love and mercy but Judah would
not listen or respond (v. 16; Jer. 5:10-13). Judgment was the only way for YHWH to purify His people and restore His plan of
revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 他们却嘻笑　神的使者，藐视他的言语，讥诮他的先知，以致耶和华的忿怒向他的百姓发作，无法可救。
verses.en: But they mocked God’s messengers, despised his warnings,[NOTE:1] and ridiculed his prophets.[NOTE:2] Finally the Lord got very angry at his people and there was no one who could prevent his judgment.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “his words.”

All three verbal forms (“mocked,” “despised,” and “ridiculed”) are active participles in the Hebrew text, indicating continual or repeated action. They made a habit of rejecting God’s prophetic messengers.
Heb “until the anger of the Lord went up against his people until there was no healer.”
verses.commentary:
36:16 "until there was no remedy" This is a sad comment. The repeated efforts of YHWH to speak to both the
kings and the people had failed. There were brief periods of incomplete repentance. The only hope for His covenant
people, His means of revelation to the nations, was judgment.

Notice the three PARTICIPLES that describe the people of Judah's repeated actions
in response to YHWH's prophets.

- mocked ‒ BDB 541, KB 532, Hiphil, cf. 2 Chr. 30:10

- despised ‒ BDB 102, KB 117, Qal

- scoffed ‒ BDB 1073, KB 1770, Hithpael (rare VERB, only twice in the OT, cf. Gen. 27:12)

The reason for YHWH's judgment is both the sins of her kings, like Manasseh, but primarily their corporate
failure to worship YHWH. They, as a culture, return again and again to the high places of Canaanite fertility worship.

verses.zh: 所以，耶和华使迦勒底人的王来攻击他们，在他们圣殿里用刀杀了他们的壮丁，不怜恤他们的少男处女、老人白叟。耶和华将他们都交在迦勒底王手里。
verses.en: He brought against them the king of the Babylonians, who slaughtered[NOTE:1] their young men in their temple.[NOTE:2] He did not spare[NOTE:3] young men or women, or even the old and aging. God[NOTE:4] handed everyone over to him.
notes: Heb “killed with the sword.”
Heb “in the house of their sanctuary.”
Or “show compassion to.”
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
36:17 "the Chaldeans" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS.

"who slew their young men. . .in the house of their sanctuary" The temple was totally defiled by the blood of the
victims (cf. Lam. 2:20; Ezek. 9:6-7). Manasseh had shed innocent blood (cf. 2 Kgs. 21:16), now YHWH allows
Nebuchadnezzar to do the same (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:4).

The fall of Jerusalem affected everyone from the young to the old. YHWH gave them all to the Babylonians
(cf. 2 Chr. 36:17-20).

YHWH had "compassion" on His people again and again (v. 15) but they would not humble themselves and
seek Him, so now He has "no compassion" (v. 17; Ezekiel 16)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

verses.zh: 迦勒底王将　神殿里的大小器皿与耶和华殿里的财宝，并王和众首领的财宝，都带到巴比伦去了。
verses.en: He carried away to Babylon all the items in God’s temple, whether large or small, as well as what was in the treasuries of the Lord’s temple and in the treasuries of the king and his officials.

verses.zh: 迦勒底人焚烧　神的殿，拆毁耶路撒冷的城墙，用火烧了城里的宫殿，毁坏了城里宝贵的器皿。
verses.en: They burned down God’s temple and tore down the wall of Jerusalem.[NOTE:1] They burned all its fortified buildings and destroyed all its valuable items.
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
36:19

NASB
"fortified buildings"

NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, Peshitta
"palaces"

JPSOA, REB
"mansions"

LXX
"bastions"

The MT has a word (BDB 74, KB 89) that is translated several ways but the basic meaning is a fortified
large home. It could be of the king, royal family, or other wealthy person. This type of building would be the first attacked and
plundered. It became a metaphor of conquest (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:18; 2 Kgs. 15:25; Ps. 122:7; Isa. 34:13; Amos 1:4,7,10,12,14).

26:17-21 The Chronicler's account of the fall of Jerusalem is much briefer than 2 Kgs. 25:1-21; also note Jer. 39:1-4;
52:4-17; and Lamentations. It is hard for modern, non-Jewish readers to imagine what the destruction of their beloved city and
temple meant to them. They surely felt no hope (i.e., Lamentations). Had YHWH abandoned His people? Israel repeatedly forgot
that the Mosaic covenant (not the Abrahamic or Davidic covenants) was conditional. The blessing flowed only through obedience.
Disobedience triggered the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28!

YHWH had a purpose for Israel, but it was an "if. . .then" covenant. YHWH wanted to reveal His character to
the nations through Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO OT COVENANT PROMISES SEEM SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?

verses.zh: 凡脱离刀剑的，迦勒底王都掳到巴比伦去，作他和他子孙的仆婢，直到波斯国兴起来。
verses.en: He deported to Babylon all who escaped the sword. They served him and his sons until the Persian kingdom rose to power.

verses.zh: 这就应验耶和华藉耶利米口所说的话：地享受安息；因为地土荒凉便守安息，直满了七十年。
verses.en: This took place to fulfill the Lord’s message spoken through Jeremiah[NOTE:1] and lasted until the land experienced[NOTE:2] its sabbatical years.[NOTE:3] All the time[NOTE:4] of its desolation the land rested in order to fulfill the seventy years.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “by the mouth of Jeremiah.”
The verb may be seen as either of two homophonous roots רָצָה (ratsah) meaning “to restore” or “to accept, take pleasure in.”

According to Lev 25:4, the land was to remain uncultivated every seventh year. Lev 26:33-35 warns that the land would experience a succession of such sabbatical rests if the people disobeyed God, for he would send them away into exile.
Heb “days of.”

Concerning the seventy years see Jer 25:11. Cyrus’ edict (see vv. 22-23) occurred about fifty years after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 b.c., which is most naturally understood as the beginning point of the “days of desolation” mentioned in v. 21. The number “seventy” is probably used in a metaphorical sense, indicating a typical lifetime and suggesting a thorough or complete judgment that would not be lifted until an entirely new generation emerged.
verses.commentary:
36:21 See exegetical notes on Jeremiah 29:10 online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

verses.zh: 波斯王塞鲁士元年，耶和华为要应验藉耶利米口所说的话，就激动波斯王塞鲁士的心，使他下诏通告全国，说：
verses.en: In the first year[NOTE:1] of King Cyrus of Persia, in fulfillment of the Lord’s message spoken through Jeremiah,[NOTE:2] the Lord motivated[NOTE:3] King Cyrus of Persia to issue a proclamation[NOTE:4] throughout his kingdom and also to put it in writing. It read:
notes: The first year of Cyrus would be ca. 539 b.c. Cyrus reigned in Persia from ca. 539-530 b.c.
See Jer 25:11; 29:10.tn Heb “by the mouth of Jeremiah.”

Heb “stirred the spirit of.” The Hebrew noun רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) has a broad range of meanings (see BDB 924-26 s.v.). Here, it probably refers to (1) “mind” as the seat of mental acts (e.g., Exod 28:3; Deut 34:9; Isa 29:24; 40:13; Ezek 11:5; 20:32; 1 Chr 28:12; cf. BDB 925 s.v. 6) or (2) “will” as the seat of volitional decisions (e.g., Exod 35:5, 22; Pss 51:12, 14; 57:8; 2 Chr 29:31; cf. BDB 925 s.v. 7). So also in Ezra 1:5. The entire phrase “stirred the spirit” has been rendered as “motivated” to better reflect normal English.

Heb “a voice.” The Hebrew noun קוֹל (qol, “voice, sound”) has a broad range of meanings, including the metonymical (cause—effect) nuance “proclamation” (e.g., Exod 36:6; 2 Chr 24:9; 30:5; 36:22; Ezra 1:1; 10:7; Neh 8:15). See BDB 877 s.v. 3.a.2.
verses.commentary:
36:22-23 This new ANE power is revealed by name (i.e., Cyrus) in Isa. 44:28 and 45:1. See The exegetical
notes online.

Cyrus was a superstitious person. He rebuilt all the temples of the gods of the nations at his expense,
so that the peoples could pray to their god for him and his successors. Judah was not the only exiled people who returned
home under Cyrus II's decree of 538 b.c.

Ezra starts with 2 Chr. 36:22-23, which shows they are connected. 2 Chronicles is the judgment but
Ezra ‒ Nehemiah the hope, as is Zechariah.

verses.zh: 「波斯王塞鲁士如此说：耶和华―天上的　神已将天下万国赐给我，又嘱咐我在犹大的耶路撒冷为他建造殿宇。你们中间凡作他子民的，可以上去，愿耶和华―他的　神与他同在。」
verses.en: “This is what King Cyrus of Persia says: ‘The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has appointed me to build a temple for him in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Anyone of his people among you may go up there, and may the Lord his God be with him.’”
verses.commentary:
36:23 "the God of heaven" See full note at Ezra 1:2.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Who are "the people of the land" in 2 Chr. 36:1?

- What did Nebuchadnezzar do with the articles from YHWH's temple?

- What does the phrase "did evil in the sight of the Lord" refer to?

- Why is 2 Chr. 36:14-16 so devastating?

- Is 2 Chr. 36:17 an example of "holy war"?

- Where does Jeremiah predict a seventy year exile? Why 70 years?

- How does 2 Chr. 36:22-23 clearly show YHWH knows the future and controls it for His purposes?

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- There is a series of faithless kings after Josiah.

- Joahaz, who reigned only three months and was replaced by Neco's surrogate (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:30-35; see Josephus,
Antiq. 10.5.2.). He was exiled to Egypt (cf. Jer. 22:11-12, where he is called "Shallum").

- Jehoiakim, Neco's surrogate (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:36-24:7) is brought in chains to Babylon (the 2 Kings parallel does not
mention this; and Jer. 22:18-19 implies he was returned quickly to Jerusalem, where he was ignobly buried; see
Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 213-214).

- Jehoiachin also reigned only three months (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:8-17; Jer. 22:24-30) and was replaced by Nebuchadnezzar's
surrogate, Zedekiah.

- Zedekiah (cf. 2 Kings 25) rebelled against Babylon, which resulted in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in
586 b.c.

- 2 Chronicles closes with a brief note about Cyrus II, King of Medo-Persia (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:1) and his allowing the Judean
exiles to return home and rebuild a much smaller temple (cf. Ezra ‒ Nehemiah).

- There were several deportations of Judeans to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar.

- 605 b.c. ‒ Jehoiakim and Daniel with his three friends

- 597 b.c. ‒ Jehoiachin and thousands of artisans

- 586 b.c. ‒ Zedekiah and the general population taken and the city of Jerusalem and the temple destroyed

- 582 b.c. ‒ at the assassination of the Babylonian-appointed Judean governor, Gedelilah, even more rural people were
deported

- See Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings, summary of these brief reigns and dates,
pp. 182-191.

1Then the people of the land took Joahaz the son of Josiah, and made him king in place of his father
in Jerusalem. 2Joahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months
in Jerusalem. 3Then the king of Egypt deposed him at Jerusalem, and imposed on the land a fine of
one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. 4The king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king
over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Joahaz his brother and brought him
to Egypt.
